This new algorithm leverages a diverse class of movements within the Euclidean group. It encompasses rotations, translations, and dilation techniques. When applied to problems with a convex potential, it is possible to prove the algorithm converges globally. Moreover, under more restrictive assumptions in problems with a non-convex potential, it is possible to prove the algorithm converges globally and yields an approximate first-order solution.

The ATLAS experiment at the LHC recorded data of 257 pb-1 in proton-proton collisions at a 5.02 TeV centre-of-mass energy in 2017, which is utilized to determine the t¯t cross-section. The measurement involves both dilepton and single-lepton t¯t final states and yields a combined result. The t¯t cross-section is found to be 67.5 pb (statistical) ± 3.6 pb (systematic) ± 0.5 pb (luminosity) pb. This corresponds to 0.265 ± 0.016 ± 0.010 pb, which is in agreement with theoretical quantum chromodynamic predictions of 66.0-76.2 pb (marginalized).

It's commonly understood that a central element of a system can exhibit ordered and chaotic behavior when connected to a disordered energy bath. Typically, the patterns of this central element repeat in a predictable manner, but certain complex systems can exhibit diverse central elements with identical patterns. We found that the central element of a disordered 3D quantum system can transition from orderly to chaotic when subjected to controlled perturbations, resulting in distinct patterns of this central element. We identified the conditions that lead to these transitions and observed unexpected relationships among these patterns. Our study provides a framework for exploring the intricate dynamics of disordered quantum systems.

The conditions on $A$, $B$, $p$, $b$, and $c$ are specified that guarantee 
${u}_{p,b,c}(z)$ meets the requirement ${u}_{p,b,c}(z) \prec (1+Az)/(1+Bz)$. This yields conditions 
for $(-4\kappa/c)({u}_{p,b,c}(z)-1)$, $c \neq 0$, to be close-to-convex and for ${u}_{p,b,c}(z)$ 
to be Janowski convex as well as $z{u}_{p,b,c}(z)$ to be Janowski convex in $z$.

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diverse range of physical and social interactions. Recent studies have begun exploring the relationship between city design, mobility, encounters, and productivity. To gain a deeper understanding of the impact of city planning, researchers employed a method that simulates urban conditions, drawing from actual cities. By developing a model that mimics face-to-face interactions in urban areas, researchers were able to analyze the effect of city design on innovation, productivity, and collaboration. Using this model, researchers discovered that a diverse and adaptable city layout tends to perform better than one optimized for efficiency. Furthermore, a more varied city tends to be more resilient against unexpected events than one with uniform characteristics.

This research project focuses on the advancement of a nonlinear field-split
preconditioner comprising two stages to expedite convergence of complex two-phase
fluid dynamics and transport within diverse porous media. A proposed algorithm,
Field-Split Newton, uses Darcy's law to quickly eliminate flow variables and
subsequently minimizes totalsurface area and mass transport differences between
phases through inner iterations. Due to its straightforward formulation and minimal
matrix factorization, this preconditioner is highly efficient and adaptable to a
variety of computational frameworks. Through a series of tests, including
single-carrier and two-phase flow simulations with intricate nonlinearities, it
has been proven that the Field-Split Newton preconditioner significantly accelerates
convergence by up to three to four times in comparison to an unpreconditioned
algorithm, while also being highly portable across various scientific computing
platforms and easy to implement.

The property of chiral light allows for the differentiation of left- and right-handed forms of chiral molecules. We have investigated the linear and nonlinear optical properties of one-dimensional photonic crystals, formed from achiral and chiral dielectric materials. The results show that while achiral photonic crystals do not discriminate between left- and right-handed forms of chiral molecules, they do not either. Conversely, we found an intrinsic ability of these photonic crystals to distinguish between the two forms. Furthermore, we found that an inhomogeneous light beam can be completely or partially polarized as it travels through the photonic crystal, depending on its composition.

This paper examines the connection between Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity on anti de-Sitter spaces and a semi-classical limit of two-dimensional string theory, with c less than 1. We observe that the world-sheet theory of this string theory, comprising a space-like Liouville CFT and a time-like non-rational CFT, exhibits actions and partition functions matching those of the JT gravity model. This match is evident beyond the Cardy limit. Furthermore, the boundary terms in the actions and partition functions, as well as the three-point functions involving the stress tensor, are identical to those of the JT gravity model. We also derive the semi-classical spectrum of the non-gaussian c less than 1 CFT, using the output of JT gravity.

A spacetime distortion, or warp bubble, generated by the Alcubierre metric can enable massive objects to achieve global speeds faster than light. This research extends our previous solutions by applying the Einstein equations to the warp drive metric, incorporating both a perfect fluid source and a perfect fluid source with a cosmological constant, including the effects of quantum gravity via the Hamilton-Jacobi formalism. For the Hamilton-Jacobi formalism, the wave equation leads to consistency requirements that effectively replicate the Einstein equations. To model quantum effects, the Hamilton-Jacobi formalism yields results analogous to those of the Klein-Gordon equation, confirming our prior findings for the massless scalar field. With a perfect fluid source, the Einstein equations are satisfied without issue, but when a perfect fluid source with a cosmological constant is used, the shift vector becomes irreducible, making the warp drive metric unfeasible.

As cities' underground systems age, they encounter increasingly severe management issues due to their intricacy and vulnerability. To address these problems, a comprehensive approach that leverages data from diverse sources and prioritizes the needs of city officials and maintenance workers is essential. This paper introduces a groundbreaking data fusion framework tailored to meet the unique demands of underground infrastructure management. Leveraging advanced data fusion techniques, our approach centralizes disparate information sources to extract valuable insights that inform key decision-making objectives. Specifically, our framework focuses on the interconnected needs of city officials and workers, enabling the creation of visualizations that showcase the structural integrity and historical records of underground structures. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, various data sources related to aging underground utilities are examined.

To analyze the center-of-mass motion of hundreds of $^9$Be$^+$ ions, arranged in a two-dimensional Wigner crystal, we utilized the interactions between laser- and microwave-induced superposition of states. By measuring the spin dephasing as a function of lateral distance from the string axis, we distinguished between effects of vibration amplitude, entanglement, and heating due to the laser used. Our study revealed a minimum level of detectable motion in the experiment, setting limits on the ion motion amplitude and the rotation frequency of strings. The results have significant implications for a variety of experiments, including quantum computations, where precise control over the string's rotation and ion arrangement is essential for achieving a precise setup.

TERS is an essential technique for analyzing surfaces with subnanometer resolution. Yet, accurately simulating TERS signals remains extremely challenging. We developed a new model that accounts for the complex interactions of the laser tip with surfaces by separating the effects of the tip and the sample. The tip's interaction with light is treated as a geometric phenomenon involving scattering and multiple reflections, while the sample's interaction with light is described using a quantum efficient detector model. By distinguishing between the sample's emission and the tip's contribution, which includes dark signals, our model effectively enhances the signal. We demonstrated the usefulness of our model in interpreting recent TERS spectra in the extreme near-field regime, characterized by substantial signal amplification due to the tip's emission.

We used the 64-m Sardinia Radio Telescope to study the emission of nearby galaxies displaying Anomalous Microwave Emission. We aimed to verify the hypothesis that AME originates from spinning, distorted dust grains. To test this, we observed 12 galaxies, including 7 spiral, 4 elliptical, and 1 irregular in shape, with frequencies ranging from 5.8 to 13.8 GHz, and ages from 0.1 to 13.8 billion years. Among these, 9 were previously known sources of AME and 5 were suspected but unconfirmed. We successfully detected AME in 9 galaxies and established a confident detection in NGC\,4631. We found evidence supporting the 'grain-rubbing' hypothesis but not the 'grain-recollision' theory. We successfully set an upper limit for the redshift of the dwarf galaxy NGC\,457. We detected synchrotron and thermal components in some of the galaxies, with particular note given to dwarf galaxies displaying radio emission but lacking a clear optical counterpart.

Ammonium sulfate experiences a unique pressure-induced phase transition
characterized by unusual stiffness and anisotropy alongside changes in
amorphization and quantum vitrification, all of which exhibit distinct responses
to increasing pressure. The shape resilience of the cation-anion network allows
it to withstand pressure up to 15 GPa without solidifying, whereas at higher
pressures it demonstrates distinct thermal behavior in different phases.

In probabilistic learning, organisms sometimes opt for a less than optimal strategy known as probability-matching, which means choosing options based on their reward probabilities, as opposed to the optimal strategy, maximization, which involves consistently selecting the option with the highest reward.  Despite years of study, the factors leading to probability-matching are still unclear and an interesting aspect is the similarity between this and maximization strategies in certain contexts, which raises the possibility of finding common genetic mechanisms underlying these behaviors.  A recent study suggests that probability-matching may be an evolutionary precursor to the maximization strategy, which is believed to be more adaptive.  The study provides evidence that the probability-matching phenomenon is not unique to humans, as it has also been observed in other organisms such as mice, rats, birds, and even zebrafish.  The researchers found that the probability-matching behavior in mice was influenced by the dopamine system's reward prediction errors and also used the calcium indicator, ArcaCor1, linked to the striatal neurons' firing patterns, which was unique to the context of probability-matching and not observed in the context of maximization.  The researchers concluded that the probability-matching behavior may be an evolutionary precursor to the more adaptive maximization strategy, which is also mediated by the same genetic mechanisms.  The researchers also hypothesized that the probability-matching behavior may also be an evolutionary precursor to other adaptive learning strategies, which require more complex decision-making processes.

A Weyl group for E8 is demonstrated to act on a K3 surface through a specific embedding, whose weight system closely mirrors that found in Miranda's work (arXiv:1807.14017), with each generator of Weyl(E8) corresponding to a certain element in the Picard group of the K3 surface. Additionally, a detailed analysis is provided of how Weyl(E7) operates on a K3 surface that lacks (1,1) curves, essentially a twisted K3 surface. Furthermore, it is shown that a particular K3 surface exhibits E8 symmetry.

The continuous Fréchet distance c-approximate near neighbor problem involves precomputing a data structure that efficiently finds closest polygonal curves within a certain radius from query curves, considering an approximation factor for potential inaccuracies. This study primarily investigates this problem using time series curves, providing a comprehensive analysis for one-dimensional curves. A new data structure, specifically tailored to time series curves, is presented and shown to achieve optimal query time, while remaining competitive in terms of space efficiency compared to existing solutions. Furthermore, lower bounds on the data structure's efficiency were established, demonstrating the impossibility of certain desired outcomes.

To mitigate systematic measurement errors on quantum computers, current methods employ counteractive postprocessing techniques. Despite effectively rectifying measurement noise, these postprocessing methods lack integration with quantum algorithms. Therefore, a new class of measurement error mitigation techniques that form an integral part of quantum algorithms are being developed. We present a novel method called repeated rounding that effectively mitigates measurement noise within the context of variational quantum algorithms. By imposing constraints on the imaginary part of the expectation value of the Hamiltonian according to the principles of the von Neumann-Taking-Algebra, we devise a set of rules governing the rounding of measurements. Moreover, by constructing a dictionary between Pauli operators and classical symmetries in the corresponding algebra, we extend its applicability to noisy quantum circuits. Our method has been successfully tested on both simulated and near-term hardware to demonstrate its efficacy.

When humans operate robots, there are often implicit rules for how they're controlled, but these norms go unexplained. This means assistants working with robots may not fully comprehend these requirements, leading to confusion and errors. To address this, we suggest that robots actively share their control protocols with operators, utilizing observed operator behavior to pinpoint areas where explanations are needed and adjusting their behavior accordingly. By doing so, robots aim to reduce overall task errors. We tested this approach, called AIDE, in simulated real-world scenarios, such as robotic surgery, finding it outperformed traditional strategies. Furthermore, robots trained using AIDE-based methods became more efficient and similar to expert human operators.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar environments independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting, but these systems often have limited capabilities to factor in high-level goals in unfamiliar areas. Research has shown that probabilistic mapping frameworks can incorporate logical variables to enable navigation systems to consider relevant information. However, existing frameworks are typically restricted to two-dimensional maps and primarily used by experienced operators. In this study, we propose a novel approach to generalise probabilistic mapping for use in multi-agent environments. We introduce a novel framework that allows robots to learn and incorporate contextual information about fellow agents and natural landmarks in three-dimensional environments. This agent- and environment-aware framework uses a unified model to incorporate contextual information and generate contextual priors. Results demonstrate that our approach significantly improves navigation in multi-agent environments compared to existing state-of-the-art methods.

Research into two-dimensional arrays with favorable two-dimensional correlation properties has gained significant interest due to the rapid advancements in modern wireless communication technologies. Various applications of two-dimensional arrays can be found within the scopes of ultra-wide band, 2-D Fourier transform spectrometry, and 2-D Hilbert transform. This paper proposes a new method for generating two-dimensional arrays with negative correlation properties by utilizing a two-dimensional generalized affine contraction lemma. The proposed method can be used to design negative correlation arrays with desired properties such as uniform amplitude, discrete phase, and variable spacing between elements, and it also allows for the optimization of various parameters within the arrays. A detailed example illustrating the proposed method is provided, and the advantages and drawbacks of this new technique are discussed compared to existing methods.

Computed Tomography (CT) is widely used for non-destructive imaging of internal structures. However, the inherent characteristics of polyenergetic X-ray sources and attenuation variability lead to artifacts such as beam hardening, which necessitates specialized image reconstruction techniques. These variations also produce disparities in X-ray transmission between adjacent regions, resulting in noticeable post-reconstruction artifacts. This phenomenon is referredly known as polyenergetic discontinuous CT (PDC-CT) effect. Although previous research primarily focused on mitigating beam hardening, the present study aims to comprehensively improve image quality by addressing both beam hardening and the PDC-CT effect. To achieve this, a novel edge beam hardening correction and PDC-CT effect removal algorithm based on edge-held reference points is proposed. Through simulations and actual experiments involving various polyenergetic X-ray sources, the suggested approach is shown to consistently surpass state-of-the-art methods in terms of overall root-mean-square error performance. Moreover, the findings reveal that the PDC-CT effect has a pronounced impact on image noise levels, with modern low-readout CT systems demonstrating significantly reduced prominence.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model.  In contrast to the local model which sometimes yields a divergence of fields, introduction of electron spillover leads to a finite transfer resistance.  Additionally, we found that hydrodynamics accurately replicates the general form of the spillover model but requires adjustment in the model parameters to precisely mirror the original behavior.  Notably, despite its simplicity, the hydrodynamics model demonstrates a more accurate representation of the spillover effect than traditional models such as Caselgrain's formula.

In this research, we investigate the user's part in Contextual Named Entity Retrieval (CNER), revealing (1) that humans outperform automated methods in pinpointing context-sensitive terms, and (2) that enhanced results can be achieved when users also specify the relative importance of those terms. Building on this discovery, we developed a novel CNER algorithm, referred to as Human-assisted CNER (HacNER. HacNER leverages the user's input by combining retrieved documents based on their overall ranking as well as their weighted selected entities. HacNER's efficacy is demonstrated through two user studies, showcasing significant improvement when utilizing the user-specified weights, yielding a 25.1% increase in precision at 8 documents. Moreover, comparing HacNER to other state-of-the-art CNER algorithms on a newly created benchmark revealed that the former surpasses the latter's performance.

Time-based data refers to information collected over a specific period, 
characterized by sudden changes, abrupt shifts, significant dimensions, 
high noise levels, and non-linear patterns. These traits are expected in 
multivariate time series data, which often exhibits linear relationships 
between variables, despite individual components following non-linear paths. 

Considering the diverse forms that time-based data can take, it is 
important to thoroughly evaluate any approach applied to it. 

Traditional methods, used for classification, forecasting, and pattern extraction, 
often fail to account for the data's complex nature. These shortcomings 
prompt innovative representations to mitigate these limitations and 
improve the handling of high-dimensional, noisy, and non-linear data. 

New representations focus on creating compact and meaningful representations 
to facilitate seamless data analysis. However, the continuous evolution of 
graph theory leads researchers to explore alternative, more robust approaches 
centered around persistence diagrams instead of linear representations. 

This shift in focus necessitates the development of novel, invariant techniques 
aimed at accurately translating global structure from original spaces to 
persistence diagrams while preserving critical topological characteristics.

Recent advancements in healthcare have led to an increase in Electronic Health Record (EHR) documentation, propelling the application of Natural Language Processing (NLP) to analyze and improve healthcare quality. A thorough examination of healthcare-related NLP research and its substantial impact on extending healthcare services is presented in this study. Initially, we provide an overview of the evolution of NLP before leveraging EHRs. Subsequently, we discuss specific practical utilization cases of NLP, such as diagnosing and predicting patient outcomes based on EHR content, and identifying pharmacological interactions and contraindications. Moreover, we explore the utilization of software tools to guide healthcare professionals' decision-making processes. Ultimately, the objective is to underscore the pivotal role of NLP in enhancing healthcare quality through data-driven decision-making.

Using a mean-field approach and considering both non-uniform dielectric profiles and ionic size, our study examines the influence of solvent polarization on the electrostatic properties of a nearby wall in an electrolyte solution. An analytical expression for the wall's dielectric function is derived near charged surfaces, and the resulting zero-order and first-order corrections to the standard Poisson-Boltzmann results are obtained. The significance of taking solvent polarization into account is demonstrated by comparing the obtained expressions with available numerical solutions.

Automating the labor-intensive and error-prone process of extracting requirements from unstructured text is a highly recommended goal for many researchers. To this end, we annotated a unique dataset, PURE, and derived a new one combining requirements and non-requirements. We refined a BERT-based model, initially trained on general text, using the updated PURE dataset, showing its potential to effectively distinguish requirements and provide additional insight with contextual information. Building upon this success, we developed an end-to-end system that efficiently extracts requirements from given texts and filters non-relevant information in three stages. The system outperformed existing state-of-the-art systems in requirement identification while also enhancing readability of the resulting output. To facilitate further research, we made the updated PURE dataset and accompanying system available online.

This study explores the interplay between maximum diversity network coding (MDNC) and energy-efficient transmission, typically achieved through power control and bit-and-piece coding. We introduce a power control strategy that simultaneously adjusts transmission power and number of helpers based on the channel state information, aiming to minimize the total transmitted power while ensuring a reliable data rate. By analyzing MDNC, we find that it offers better energy efficiency compared to no network coding. Furthermore, we propose a power control algorithm using MDNC and bit-and-piece coding that outperforms alternative schemes, including those using MDNC alone or bit-and-piece coding alone. Additionally, we present a power control algorithm using MDNC in the absence of channel state information, demonstrating improved energy efficiency and higher data rates compared to other relevant works.

A superconducting surface with strategically positioned magnetic impurities hosts Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states, which serve as localized Andreev states. These impurities can be thought of as tiny magnetic flags indicating superconductivity strength, their density allowing for detailed analysis of the superconducting correlation length. Due to their proximity to each other, their magnetic fields interact and influence one another, particularly when in pairs, resulting in a merged magnetic structure. As paired magnetic impurities are placed at the surface of a superconductor, their combined magnetic field reduces correlation length measurement precision, a problem also applicable to the uniform magnetic chain formed during the BCS transition, being replaced by a chain of isolated magnetic impurities. These magnetic impurities, formed during the pairing process, can recreate the precision issue observed in the impurity pair. However, our findings reveal an additional mechanism reducing correlation length measurement precision: paired magnetic impurities, even when separated, can create a uncertainty principle-like effect, known as flux noise, restricting precise correlation length measurement. These mechanisms, independently examined in the models of two impurities and magnetic chains, display comparable characteristics, including equivalent noise scales, impurity separation effects, and shapes, suggesting similar physics in both models and the uniform magnetic chain formed during the BCS transition, a model independently examined in the study.

Techniques such as the Normal Distributions Transform (NDT) can efficiently register and accurately bound point cloud errors for scenes without moving objects.  However, traditional methods struggle in scenes where there are changes in view.  A deep learning-based solution, Deep NDT, was previously developed to register and bound point clouds for dynamic scenes, but it has limitations, including requiring access to ground truth registration and point cloud data.  A novel approach, deep local registration, is introduced to accurately bound point cloud errors for dynamic scenes, and validate its effectiveness by comparing it to both traditional methods and the Deep NDT approach, using publicly available datasets.  Additionally, it demonstrates better performance than other current state-of-the-art methods for point cloud registration.  A supporting video can be found at https://youtu.be/-L9s9b8jC9g.

Satellite images are widely employed across multiple sectors, encompassing 
agriculture, navigation, and urban planning, often resulting in immense 
databases requiring extensive computational power for manual analysis.

Subjecting materials to intense, pulsed X-ray radiation allows for in-depth analysis of their electronic properties, as changes in electronic structures become apparent beyond a certain dose threshold. The method, known as time-resolved XANES, has been used to investigate Pr valence transitions in La$_{2-x}$Pr$_x$NiO$_4$ and Ba$_{1-x}$Pr$_x$TiO$_3$, where varying conditions resulted in distinct electronic state populations. The distinct behavior is attributed to differences in the target geometry, initial electronic state distribution, and their respective degrees of freedom, which significantly influence the degree of electronic excitation induced by the X-ray pulse. This investigation provides a comprehensive comparison and correlation of various experimental parameters, providing valuable insights into reference systems for the analysis of dynamic semiconductor band edge transitions.

The application of Deep Neural Networks (DNN) has significantly enhanced the efficiency of automatic modulation classification (AMC) in wireless systems. However, current surface-based DNN approaches suffer from high computational complexity and limited capability to function effectively in situations where training data is scarce or missing. In contrast, traditional deep learning methods, such as the data-driven DNN approach, require extensive computational resources and time. In an effort to improve the efficiency of AMC while minimizing computational requirements, we introduce a new classification method called the hybrid DNN approach. This new method first applies a surface-based DNN to identify potentially relevant sub-surfaces, thus narrowing down the data set for a second DNN model to improve efficiency. Notably, our hybrid DNN method outperforms current surface-based and data-driven DNN approaches in terms of accuracy and computational requirements.

Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is crucial for assessing disease progression and evaluating treatment effectiveness. While current deep learning techniques excel at lesion segmentation, they can be unreliable when confronted with contrasting information in complex cases. Building on the successful results of bilateral fusion in single lesion segmentation, we developed the Bilateral Multiple Sclerosis Lesion Segmentation (BMSLS) model. Our innovative approach involves fusing three dimensions of information - conventional radiology, advanced ENLoG segmentation, and bilateral learning. To address the significant gap between training and clinical applications, we employed data augmentation, optimized hyperparameters, and assessment metrics. Our BMSLS model demonstrates remarkable efficiency, accurately segmenting 94.4% of lesions on an independent test dataset with an average dice coefficient of 0.80, thus outperforming state-of-the-art models.

A novel type of metric comparison analogous to Alexandrov comparison is established, 
and its relationship to optimal transport between measures on a Riemannian manifold 
is demonstrated, specifically with respect to the MTW condition proposed by Xi-Nan 
Ma, Neil Trudinger and Xu-Jia Wang, involving a notion of continuity.

Building on the recent findings of J. H. M\"uller, we've explored the non-asymptotic generalization error in black-box modeling of continuous-time systems, where we've also derived a tight bound on the generalization error in terms of the sampling interval $T$ and a specific dimensionality measure for the output space, yielding an error bound of $\Gamma(T) \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}$. This newly developed error bound streamlines existing high-frequency approximation methods in functional analysis and demonstrates their connection to C. Fefferman's recent results on kernel approximation, which were initially applied to continuous-time systems.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows, specifically protostellar and starless cores.  Protostellar cores are found to possess greater mass than their starless counterparts, with mass discrepancies holding true even after correcting for factors like temperature and opacity.  We interpret this observed mass difference as a sign of mass growth among cores, with far-reaching implications for the origin of massive star formation.  In essence, it challenges the conventional view that massive star formation must originate from massive prestellar cores.  Further research is necessary to fully explore the mass function of prestellar cores, specifically one that might be hidden within the molecular outflow population.

The theoretical primordial black holes that may have formed in the early universe are proposed as a possible type of dark matter. If these black holes exist, they can potentially be identified through specific astronomical phenomena. Two possible indicators are the radiation emitted as a result of the process of superradiance, as well as the decay of Planckian black holes. The superradiance signal has a more limited detection scope, whereas Planckian decay signals cover a broader range but are less intense. Combining these three types of signals allows for a more comprehensive search than would be possible with either set of signals alone. Using current astronomical data, researchers have searched for signs of these black hole decays but have found no such evidence. This search has ruled out the existence of a significant portion of primordial black holes.

We conducted research into systems at equilibrium consisting of uniform wedge-shaped molecules using Monte Carlo simulations, where each molecule consisted of multiple soft disks attached at specific points, denoted as $s$. Varying the number of disks changed the shape of the molecules, with five disks creating isosceles triangular shapes, and larger numbers of disks forming cylindrical shapes at high endibilities. We examined the effects of packing density, number of molecules, temperature, and shape flexibility on liquid crystalline order and entropic effects. At low packing densities (less than 0.5), we observed smectic and nematic phases, with increasing molecular count inducing a transition from the smectic nematic phase to the standard nematic phase. For highly flexible molecules (with 11 disks), we found nematic and columnate phases at high temperatures and nematic and smectic phases at lower temperatures. We discovered a new nematic-columnate phase transition with increasing molecular count, accompanied by a competition between entropic effects and mesophases.

Our goal with parameter-efficient tuning is to minimize updates to model parameters
when adapting a pre-trained model to downstream tasks. This paper proposes PASTA,
where we adjust only the special token embeddings, like separator and classification tokens in BERT, just before self-attention operations in each Transformer layer.
By doing this, PASTA can achieve performance on par with fine-tuning for natural language understanding tasks such as text categorization and named entity recognition while updating a mere 0.029% of all parameters. Our contribution offers a straightforward yet efficient way to fine-tune pre-trained models, requiring significantly fewer updates (0.029% vs. 11.95%) and significantly fewer training steps (16 vs. 80) in comparison to previous methods like BERT-PFT. Furthermore, PASTA surpasses performance of BERT-PFT, achieving an exact match of accuracy on IMDB (accuracy: 97.73%) and CoNLL-2003-NER (F1: 90.21).

This paper investigates a complex problem where we need to assess the impact of adding items to a collection. The inherent nature of this problem prevents us from making absolute preferences, which means we have to rely on relative rankings. To tackle this issue, we propose using a type of Siamese neural network architecture that allows us to compare two sets containing different sizes after a certain number of elements have been added. Our work builds upon the foundation laid by Siamese models in facial recognition and similarity learning. However, our novel approach differs significantly from existing ones, as we're focused on categorical rankings rather of set additions. To validate our method's effectiveness, we've established a relevant dataset called SetRanking1000+ and performed various experiments to demonstrate its practical applications. These experiments include analyzing user preferences for 100+ items, studying user additions to a digital shopping basket, and examining user preferences for 5000+ items, among others. Our results reveal that our approach can provide accurate preferences with low variation, especially in scenarios involving large numbers of items.

Our application of the lattice cluster theory for polymer fluids has established that the distinctions between configurational entropy, enthalpy, and internal energy vanish in accordance with the principles of thermodynamics. This finding, however, contradicts the widely held assumption in molecular dynamics simulations that these properties remain disjoint. As a result, we developed an approach that incorporates the lattice cluster theory within the framework of thermodynamic paths, thereby supporting this notion that these properties do not overlap. This conclusion is further substantiated by examining the case of Lennard-Jones polymers, a scenario characterized by exceptionally high complexity levels equivalent to 100 and above.

Transformer-based language models have been shown to struggle with logical reasoning, especially when it involves negation. Unlike previous studies that relied on psycholinguistic tools, our research delves into types of negation from developmental psychology, such as negation of existentials and negation of universals. We create a test based on existing datasets from experiments in developmental psychology, adapting it for language models to evaluate their ability to reason with negation. The test consists of two parts, involving the same action but with different types of negation, aiming to identify action verbs that, when combined with the same negation type, result in the same meaning as a related verb. The test reveals that models like T5 and Flamingo perform significantly better on the test for negation of universals than on the test for negation of existentials, suggesting a consistent model behavior. Moreover, our research indicates a strong connection between the performance of models in the negation of universals task and their ability to accurately answer questions regarding properties of existentials, as measured by their performance on existing datasets.

In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT19 German-to-English translation tasks.

We derive formulas for the weights of Kontsevich graphs that emerge from connections, curvatures, and Lie derivatives of symplectic manifolds, with a simplified visualization of the corresponding structures in Kontsevich's graph expansion.

This research involves determining the large N limit of $O(N)$ models with non-polynomial potential functions in odd dimensional spaces, leading to a new class of interacting conformal field theories. Specifically, this results in CFTs for dimensions 3+4n where n is a positive integer. Calculations of thermal entropy are also carried out for these same dimensions and time periods. It was discovered that in 2+1 dimensions, the ratio of strong-to-weak thermal entropy is 4/5, confirming prior results, and a similar analysis was applied to higher dimensions. An analysis of vacuum entanglement entropy was performed across multiple dimensions and it was found that in large N limits, this value approaches a constant for various potentials. Interestingly, this constant is proportional to $\log N$ for certain potential functions and to $1/N$ for others.

Cai, Song and Kou made a significant contribution in 2015 with the development of a universal approach for pricing Asian options based on one-dimensional Markov processes. This note applies Markov's property to continuous-time Markov chains for a more precise calculation, resulting in a universal explicit formula for the reduced processes of Markov's property. Moreover, this formula can be used to derive explicit solutions to the second-order partial integro-differential equations of Cai, Song and Kou.

The source behind the diffuse gamma-ray background is currently unknown. However, various galactic features such as star-forming and starburst galaxies, black holes, and cosmic clusters may all play a part in this phenomenon. Researchers conducted a study that simulated how cosmic rays interact within galactic clusters using cosmological magnetohydrodynamical models. Their analysis, spanning a range of redshift values, suggests that clusters of galaxies could account for up to 100 percent of the gamma-ray flux measured by Fermi-LAT at energy levels above 100 GeV, assuming certain conditions are met. Specifically, these conditions include specific spectral indices and energy cutoffs, and clusters of a certain mass and redshift. Their predictions also anticipate future observations of high-energy gamma-rays from clusters using upcoming experiments like CTA.

Extra energy injected by primordial features in inflationary models can generate massive particles exceeding the Hubble scale during inflation. This prospect expands the scope of cosmological collider physics, where the signals produced by these particles are usually suppressed by the Boltzmann distribution. Our analysis explores the mechanics of a cosmic collider through two types of primordial features. Firstly, we consider oscillating primordial features, encompassing cases of massive field oscillations and oscillatory features in the inflationary potential. Secondly, we examine features induced by sub-Planckian excitations of inflammatory fields. In the latter case, the exotic particle's mass is indicated by a negative value, capping the particle's mass at the inflationary scale. Our analysis indicates that the cosmic collider signal can dominate over the Boltzmann distribution suppression, resulting in detectable signs from oscillatory features with masses exceeding 10% of the inflationary scale or sub-Planckian excitations with masses less than the inflationary scale.

Understanding the decisions made by visual models is crucial, as it enables confident deployments in high-stakes environments. However, our research reveals that state-of-the-art visual models, including those utilized in practice, lack clear interpretability. In this study, we introduce a new measure of interpretability and create synthetic data with an extremely simple decision-making rule. By designing models that are both accurate and transparent, we hope to inspire new approaches that combine effective visual perception with understandable machine learning models.

Developing a simplified microscopic model of cuprates is crucial in uncovering the mechanism behind high-temperature superconductivity. By comparing our simulation results with a recent photoemission spectroscopy study of one-dimensional cuprate chains, we have discovered that long-range electron-phonon coupling plays a significant role in the formation of the hybridized band. However, we have also found that short-range electron interactions, rather than long-range interactions, drive the Fermi level to shift towards the larger hole bandwidth, mimicking the actual cuprate composition. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that using model electrons with repulsive interactions alongside phonons enables us to accurately recreate observed band structure and spectral patterns. These findings validate the feasibility of our model in simplifying the complex physics of cuprate superconductors and highlight the crucial cooperative effects of electrons and phonons in high-temperature superconductors.

A positive factor contributing to HIV prevention is widespread awareness.  However, there remains a need to determine whether such awareness translates into protective behavior, and what influences awareness levels among the general population. This study examined the relationship between demographic characteristics, personal beliefs, and HIV knowledge among high school students in Kenya, using a sample selected through a stratified, two-stage process. The results showed that both government support and access to education play crucial roles in ensuring HIV knowledge among female students. In contrast, HIV knowledge among male students is linked to factors such as government support and access to education, as well as cultural beliefs regarding the disease. The analysis also suggested that government policies play a significant part in promoting HIV knowledge among the general population. The results imply that while government policies, cultural norms, and access to education are vital factors in HIV prevention, there remains significant disparity in HIV knowledge gaps in Kenya, necessitating targeted interventions to promote HIV prevention and reduce gender-based disparities.

In the chiral magnet Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$ of $\beta$-Mn type, it's discovered that the transition from a metastable skyrmion lattice at room temperature to an equilibrium helical state below 120 K, occurs through the growth of domains with a helical order instead of a long-range skyrmion lattice. This unusual phase transition is attributed to external disorder that hinders the formation of a large-domain helical state. As a result, the metastable skyrmion state is short-lived, breaking down into multiple isolated magnetic bubbles. This unusual ground state is confirmed through the exploration of its magnetic and topological characteristics.

High-Dimensional Dynamic Factor Models are thoroughly explored, covering key 
assumptions and their underlying rationales, significant outcomes, and example
exhibits through simple demonstrations. The theory and implementation of 
these models, focusing specifically on singular ARMA models, prioritizing clarity 
over comprehensive coverage of the current literature.

The equilibrium problem described by the Nikaid\^o-Isoda-Fan inequality encompasses several key problems like optimization, variational inequality, and others, as specific instances. This paper aims to provide a clear outline illustrating the connection between fixed points of the Moreau proximal mapping and solutions to the equilibrium problem that satisfy particular monotonicity and Lipschitz-type constraints.

Deep learning's strong empirical performance stems from its capacity for representing and distinguishing between uncertain predictions.  A predictive model's output is comprised of both aleatoric uncertainty, which is stochastic in nature, and epistemic uncertainty, which is entirely random.  To improve performance and speed up training, Bayesian deep learning aims to separate and manage these two sources of uncertainty.  However, accurately distinguishing between uncertainty has been a challenging task, particularly in situations with limited data.  To address this limitation, our approach leverages an ensemble method using multiple models, trained on different subsets of available data.  Each individual model is trained using a small subset of data, with the rest held private for testing purposes.  By training multiple models on different data, we effectively introduce both aleatoric and epistemic uncertainties into our predictions.  To quantify the magnitude of each type of uncertainty, we employ predictive uncertainty metrics, calculated from each model's predictive distribution.  To further refine our predictions, we apply a filtering method, which aims to eliminate excess uncertainty based on a measure of epistemic uncertainty.  When tested across several benchmark datasets, our approach for UDA-based Bayesian deep learning has yielded a new state-of-the-art standard for quantitative uncertainty estimation and improved performance, particularly in situations with limited data.

The debate on turbulent effects influencing magnetic activity in the Sun and stars persists. The mean-field theory provides a widely applied framework to link these effects to fundamental magnetohydrodynamics, although it's not possible to observe these effects directly. To gain insight, researchers utilize global convective dynamo simulations to investigate turbulent effects by using magnetohydrodynamic equations based on transport coefficients derived from turbulent energy and length scales. In this study, we aimed to identify the underlying mechanisms driving the variation of turbulent transport coefficients in simulations of the Sun's convective zone. In order to achieve this, we used a global convective dynamo simulation of the Sun to study the dynamic changes of turbulent transport coefficients and their relation to the solar cycle. We found that coefficients related to energy and momentum transport show distinct changes, while coefficients related to magnetic transport showed an unexpected response. In the simulations, we observed an initial increase in energy-related coefficients and magnetic transport coefficients, followed by a decline as the cycle progressed. In contrast, we observed a reverse pattern in momentum transport coefficients. These findings suggest that coefficients are highly influenced by variations in turbulent kinematic and dynamic properties, as well as by changes in the existing magnetic field and its effects on the solar convective zone.

We conducted a comprehensive study using ALMA's high-sensitivity capabilities, measuring CO(0-1), CO(1-0), and CO(2-1) emission towards the galaxy NGC4945. Our goal was to identify molecular outflows produced by gas outpoured from the galaxy's nucleus. We analyzed the emission patterns and velocities of these outflows, noting that some outflows appear as head-tail structures, featuring high-velocity gas. We used specific emission lines to calculate gas velocities and estimated the fastest outflow at approximately 930 km/s. We analyzed the emission patterns and velocities, noting that some outflows appear as narrow, high-velocity gas filaments. We used VLA radio observations to calculate the gas kinetic energy and radiative pressure of the outflows, finding that kinetic energy and pressure values significantly exceed star formation expectations. We used gas outflow models, taking into account the outflows' geometry and velocity, to estimate the outflows' mechanical energy release. We calculated the mechanical energy release of the outflows, noting that they can account for up to half of the galaxy's energy budget for star formation. We used gas outflow models to estimate the outflows' effect on the galaxy's surrounding medium, noting that the outflows can push gas away from the galaxy's center, creating a gas cavity. We used gas outflow models to estimate the outflows' effect on the galaxy's surrounding metal content, specifically the metal abundance of the gas. We

A comprehensive theory is developed for the resonant interaction between particles and waves in a magnetized plasma, taking into account the full complexity of its dispersion relation. The model represents the plasma as a turbulent, disordered medium composed of diverse species, and incorporates an electromagnetic field that is dynamic and coupled with this medium. The concept of resonant interaction is generalized to encompass a wide range of physical processes, and the electron distribution is specified using a kinetic model. The theory is applied to the specific case of the Earth's magnetosphere, and the conditions necessary for resonant interaction are identified. The existence of turbulent, dynamic electromagnetic fields in the magnetosphere provides the basis for broadband electrostatic waves and the potential for their growth through resonant interaction. The kinetic model used for electron distribution results in energy dissipation and the heating of the plasma, as well as the cooling of specific populations, and the formation of beam distributions. The developed theory provides a useful framework for simulating and understanding various processes in the magnetosphere, including the composition of the plasmas and the energy distribution of the particles.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by introducing variable stepsize SGLMs. These new methods encompass linear methods with order p ≥ 2 and stage order r ≥ 1. We present convergence properties for SGLMs under the most flexible nonlinear convergence condition. Furthermore, we illustrate the design and implementation of nonlinear SGLMs with variable stepsize using the Nordsieck technique via numerical convolutions. Additionally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of these new methods through numerical experiments on several test problems.

We provide a relationship between the exponential stability of a C0-semigroup T and solutions of a specific Lyapunov inequality in B+(X,X*), where X is a Banach space. The inequality's solutions determine the boundedness of the resolvent R(λ,A) inside and outside the left half-plane and left invertibility of T, the C0-semigroup.

This paper introduces MuMuPy, a computational software and web-based tool for determining the interaction cross sections between dimuonium (true muonium) and matter, also computing corresponding form factors. With MuMuPy, users can estimate the likelihood of dimuonium transitioning within an atomic nucleus' electric field, transversely aligning its orbital and spin states. Developed primarily in Python with a focus on efficiency, MuMuPy incudes both command-line interfaces and a web-based interface for interactive calculations. It allows for precise calculations of interaction probabilities between dimuonium and nuclei across a broad range of masses and charges. Additionally, MuMuPy offers methods for determining nuclear form factors and weak and electromagnetic muonium-nucleus transitions. Available in open-source format, MuMuPy is highly adaptable and easily integratable into larger-scale simulations. It is suitable for educational and research use, particularly in physics, nuclear and particle, and muon muon experiments.

Portfolio managers assess investment success in relation to market standards, specifically using the Standard & Poor 500 index as a benchmark. Our revised assessment combines two key measures: the portfolio's absolute value and its performance relative to that of a chosen benchmark. The traditional Merton problem, however, solely focuses on the portfolio's absolute wealth. In contrast, our modified problem accounts for the dependence between a client's absolute wealth and the performance of the portfolio relative to the benchmark. The client seeks to minimize the probability of the portfolio losing to both the absolute standard and the benchmark, often at a higher rate. Through a mathematical approach using a specific type of differential equation, we analyze this modified optimization problem and derive key outcomes. We validate the applicability of the results by comparing them with findings from existing research, specifically in relation to a scenario known as the vanishing benchmark.

The most abundant galaxy type in the cosmos is dwarf galaxies, which exhibit distinct characteristics when compared to larger, brighter counterparts. This article centers on the physical and chemical properties of the interstellar material within dwarf galaxies containing notable quantities of gas and dust. The discussion includes the characteristics of neutral and ionized gases, the effects of dust, and initial evidence suggesting the presence of Active Galactic Nuclei (AGN) in the nucleus of certain galaxies. The article also compares the properties of the interstellar material in dwarf galaxies to those found in larger, spiral-shaped counterparts, and explores the material's evolution across various stages, from star-forming to quiescent. Furthermore, the article touches on the unique characteristics of ultra-diffuse galaxies, which lack prominent stellar structures, and speculate on the potential consequences of their observed properties.

We investigate the stability of fermionic quasiparticles in a fermion-boson model based on a Bethe lattice, where fermions interact with local bosons through a Peierls coupling. By reducing the complex model into a non-interacting chain with varying site potentials, we demonstrate that despite the presence of multiple bosonic excitations costing zero energy, the quasiparticle is resistant to destruction. The stability of the quasiparticle emerges as a consequence of the extensive entropy associated with the chain's relevant variables, which arises due to the extensive nature of the bosonic zero-energy excitations. We discover the thresholds for the interaction exponents, beyond which the quasiparticle loses stability. Interestingly, the upper critical exponent value turns out to be twice the lower critical value. Furthermore, we explore various generalizations of the model, including those simulating Peierls coupling, as well as the effects of non-Abelian bosonic excitations and fermionic pair-hopping interactions.

Golan and Sapir \cite{MR3978542} showed that the Thompson's groups $F$, $T$, and $V$ exhibit linear divergence. The present work extends this analysis to Thompson's subgroups. Notably, we find that subgroups associated with $V$ have a linear divergence as well. Additionally, we establish that certain subgroups of $T$ possess exponential divergence.

This paper demonstrates the end-to-end fine-tuning of the Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) architecture. Key technical hurdles are identified that must be overcome to accomplish this goal. A comparative evaluation is presented to show the superiority of the end-to-end RAG architecture in the context of question answering. Our implementation of the end-to-end RAG architecture has been made publicly available on the HuggingFace Transformers library.

This study calculates the long-term behavior of the orthogonal polynomials relative to a logarithmic weight directly from a formula that sums a polynomial and its preceding term, multiplied by a weight function that varies logarithmically with the variable $x$. The investigation also explores connections between these polynomials and a special type of function known as the Riemann $L$-function at $s=1$, and demonstrates how behaviors in both the complex plane and on the real axis mirror one another. Additionally, specific data on the polynomials' zeros near a critical point and their asymptotic behavior, along with details about associated integrals, are derived and show consistency with established conjectures in the field.

Utilizing crowdsourcing platforms like Amazon Mechanical Turk to acquire top-tier human annotations proves more complicated than initially thought, influenced by several key factors, such as task instructions and annotator compensation, among others. To prevent inaccurate annotations which could mislead automatic summarization systems, we develop and implement a multi-stage recruitment process targeting high-quality MTurk workers. By establishing a rigorous evaluation pipeline, we demonstrate the ability to exclude unskilled annotators prior to data collection, resulting in significantly improved annotation quality when compared to unstructured recruitment. Specifically, our approach yields skilled annotators who demonstrate strong consistency in annotating news summaries in line with expert evaluations, thereby facilitating the establishment of a robust training dataset for a reliable summarization system.

Text-video retrieval, a crucial task in multimedia processing, has seen significant advancement with the emergence of pre-trained vision-language models. Nonetheless, existing methods still face challenges when dealing with text queries containing typos or linguistic irregularities. To tackle this issue, we introduce the TS2-Net, a novel approach that incorporates a token shift module. This module allows for a flexible reordering of text tokens and is seamlessly integrated into the text encoder. By adapting the text encoder to accommodate token manipulation, we effectively enhance the compatibility of text-video retrieval with queries featuring altered token arrangements. Thorough experiments and evaluations conducted on three benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of our approach.

We've found that neutral flavour-changing currents in top sector physics, linked to electroweak scale particles that interact with leptons, are more plausible than previously thought, given the LHC's standard model-like Higgs searches and top quark measurements. Our analysis centers around the novel NCFCNC processes involving a top quark, a bottom quark, and a lepton $\bar{t} \bar{b} \ell^-$. It appears these processes have been overlooked and could be sensitive to new physics. Our searches set limits on the coupling between leptophilic scalars and top quarks, even under relatively conservative assumptions. Moreover, when considering a linear connection between flavour profiles and colour representations, our constraints significantly restrict the parameter space for several colour triplets and colour octets.

In response to the intricacies of network data, a new type of hybrid network is suggested. This hybrid network combines elements of preferential attachment and uniform attachment rules. In a study, it was found that a mixture of these rules, according to a specific weight ratio, produces a fractal network. In particular, a regime near the preferential attachment dominant zone yields a self-similar network with a specific set of repeating patterns. This phenomenon indicates a potential method to create artificial networks with desired fractal properties. Conversely, the mixture also enables the analysis of real-world networks using fractal dimension as an additional analytical tool. Ultimately, this approach can be used for various applications, such as predicting the behavior of artificial hybrid networks and evaluating the self-similar structure of real-world networks.

The growing number of users in wireless communications leads to interference problems that cannot be resolved by traditional means, making reliable data transmission more challenging. To address these issues effectively, reliable wireless connections must be established, even in the presence of interference. This research focuses on developing new methods for detecting, identifying, and mitigating multiple types of interference, such as RSSI, LORAN-C, DSSS, and LBT, through advanced image processing techniques. By utilizing deep neural networks, it is possible to accurately detect and identify different signals, while neural networks specifically designed for image processing tasks enable precise geolocation and enable the development of adaptive interference mitigation strategies. By managing wireless interference and ensuring reliable data transmission, the proposed methods aim to prevent accidents in safety-critical industries by accurately detecting and localizing devices.

To grasp the impact of gravitational fields on quantum systems, we suggest a quantum particle confined to a square potential subject to weak vertical illumination, accompanied by an analysis of its bound and unbound states. Upon introducing a particle in the well, its energy levels adjust to account for the effects of a uniform vertical illumination, thereby yielding their average values. Next, we consider the case of an unbound state, where we resolve a partial differential equation to obtain a probability distribution, calculate its expectation value, and interpret the findings in relation to a particle falling under the influence of gravity.
Countable, locally standard measure algebras are parameterized by a pair of Steinitz numbers, consisting of one value which equals or exceeds 1.

Parton distributions inside a nucleon can be understood in relation to a correlation between quarks and gluons through generalized parton distributions, which are the key components of the nucleon's parton model description.  Initially, researchers explored individual functions describing twist-2 behavior.  However, studying the interplay between functions in the same argument varies based on the state of spin, which is associated with the nucleon's state of motion.  Investigating this relationship requires calculating all combinations of PDFs including their differences.  Notably, researchers discovered an anomaly in the sum rule condition for the so-called cross-function, which is the twist-2 gluon PDF for a nucleon at zero momentum transfer.  Two possible explanations, namely a mistake in the sum rule formula derived from the parton model description or a defect in the sum rule itself, are being investigated further to determine the source of the discrepancy.  In contrast, the sum rule condition for the nucleon's twist-2 quark PDF is consistent with predictions from the parton model description.  Calculations using various nucleon models, including the bag model, support the correct sum rule, which is the norm for nucleon's twist-2 quark PDFs.  In light of these results, researchers suggest revisiting the understanding of parton correlations, specifically the nature of partons, which are currently considered point-like but may, in fact, be extended objects with spatial extent due to inter-parton interactions.

All AI systems inevitably make mistakes, characterized by their unpredictability and distinctness from human errors. A critical objective is to rectify these AI errors without compromising their established abilities and ideally without requiring direct human intervention. This report outlines an innovative approach aimed at enhancing the performance of existing AI systems in specific areas by temporarily adjusting their behavior to prevent undesirable outcomes. This approach involves creating temporary rules that can be automatically identified using automated evaluation methods. By promoting continuous learning and adaptation, this methodology capitalizes on the strengths of both machine-powered systems and human intuition, thereby ensuring that corrected AI agents remain efficient and efficient. Furthermore, this approach demonstrates significant potential in addressing complex issues, such as minimizing harm and maximizing social interactions, and can be effectively applied to diverse domains, including systems that operate autonomously.

Our research involves exploring the thermal behavior of the Bose-Hubbard model in systems with spin-orbit coupling as influenced by external magnetic fields. Specifically, we examine how the effective mass of bosons is impacted by Rashba and Rabi interactions in external magnetic fields. Our analysis shows that an increase in Rashba spin-orbit coupling or Rabi coupling results in a stronger critical interaction required to achieve the superfluid-Mott insulator phase transition. Additionally, we find that applying a magnetic field perpendicular to the plane of Rashba coupling can drive the superfluid and valence-bond phase of paired bosons to transition into a Mott insulator. However, when the magnetic field is parallel to the Rashba coupling, we observe minimal changes in phase diagrams until very high magnetic field strengths are reached, thereby offering tolerance against fluctuations.

Consider two groups, G_1 and G_2, and suppose a homomorphism \phi from G_1 to G_2 maps a particular element to another element. In the context of graph theory, this leads to the concept of graph degeneration, which is then explored in the realm of group algebra. The set algebra corresponding to a graph G is defined as the linear combination of its vertex sets. Graph image under this algebra corresponds to the homomorphism between the group algebras, thus providing a theoretical basis for graph homomorphism. The question of whether a graph can be reduced to another by erasing vertices or edges is addressed in terms of group algebra morphisms. The notion of elementary group algebra degeneration is also proposed, involving the deletion of a single vertex. The element-embedding property is examined to understand whether a vertex can be embedded in another graph, which leads to the concept of vertex degeneration. The study focuses on whether different forms of graph degeneration correspond to group degeneration, which involves the homomorphism between the group algebras, and whether these different forms can lead to the same reduced graph. The investigation also delves into the non-existence issue of elementary group algebra degeneration.

Recent breakthroughs in AdS/CFT correspondence research, specifically in low-dimensional settings, are explored, concentrating on AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ and AdS$_2$/CFT$_1$ dualities within massive Type IIA string theory. Both the supersymmetric sigma models derived from target space actions and dual superconformal theories in the context of supergravity describe distinct dual pair relationships. These involve primary duals consisting of string theory's classical solutions and their associated Green-Schwarz superstrings, as well as secondary duals formed through supergravity perturbations and GS-string superstrings. Pseudo-Nijenhuis (dual to holomorphic flows) and Eliashberg dualities constitute the two categories of secondary duals. Each duality manifests differently at the supersymmetric CFT$_2$ level for AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ and CFT$_1$ levels for AdS$_2$/CFT$_1$, influenced by distinct super twists. By examining quasi-conformal supergravity expansions, we investigate the structure of the pseudo-Nijenhuis duals' associated superconformal theorems and their connections to KZ-cohomology.

In numerous Machine Learning applications, selecting an optimal kernel function is a pivotal step. Gaussian Processes excel in regression and classification tasks, largely depending on a suitable kernel function. Traditionally, Gaussian Process researchers have chosen standard kernel functions or modified them. This study employs a Genetic-Programming algorithm to automatically discover kernel functions, resulting in more accurate and versatile Gaussian Process models. By embedding Gaussian kernels, we can maintain the benefits of standard kernels while enhancing their capabilities. Our method allows automatic kernel construction, yielding precise Gaussian Process models. Experimental results validate the success of our proposed algorithm, yielding performance superior to current methods.

Future high-energy muon colliders pose a significant challenge in terms of beam-induced background control, which can lead to excessive background counts and hinder detector capabilities. In the context of the Muon Collider, the current understanding of detector requirements suggests that minimal viable detector design must be able to handle background rates of up to 1 kHz per beam. One promising concept for addressing this issue involves the early detection and deflection of muons near the interaction point, followed by a precise muon reconstruction in a larger drift tube tracker. In this study, we simulate and evaluate the performance of this concept within the detector framework established in the MuCICLO study. Notably, our results indicate that this concept is capable of reducing background rates to around 200-300 events per second per beam, closely meeting the strict requirements of the detector.

Introducing Spartan, a novel approach for training neural networks with pre-defined sparsity. Spartan combines the strengths of two techniques, supermasking and superconductance, offering flexibility in adapting to varying sparsity patterns. Supermasking introduces initial constraints on pruned parameters, while superconductance fine-tunes this sparsity mask during training. Spartan's framework allows for seamless integration of both techniques, making it suitable for different scenarios, such as initial random or learned supermasks, as well as variable levels of sparsity, ranging from a few to nearly fully connected. Spartan's effectiveness is demonstrated through sparsity and accuracy assessments on multiple datasets and models, showcasing its superiority over state-of-the-art methods and various benchmark experiments. Spartan's code and configuration files can be found on GitHub at https://github.com/adiir/sparian.

The emergence of one-dimensional (1D) behavior in systems involving ultracold atoms offers a versatile platform to examine collectivistic properties. Our investigation focuses on the development of thermalization in a 1D Bose gas as an examination of many-body interaction-driven processes. Theoretical models, including Bose-Einstein condensation and Bogoliubov excitations, are utilized to analyze low- and high-density states. Theoretical predictions are validated through one, two, and three-dimensional simulation scenarios. The conversion of a three-dimensional Bose gas to a 1D Bose gas is studied through numerical simulations, revealing an intermediate regime characterized by multidimensional behavior. The 1D Bose gas thermalization process is shown to be significantly influenced by initial dimensional adaptation, thereby providing a critical time frame for observing multidimensional characteristics.

Software developers widely acknowledge the importance of unit testing, yet few pay attention to the quality of the test code, which can be poorly written. Test smells, analogous to code smells found in software, negatively impact the maintainability of test code. Detecting these smells manually is an inefficient task, which is why experts have created several automated test smell detection tools. However, their methods typically focus on individual test files or overlook relevant file-level characteristics. Our research introduces T5S, an innovative tool capable of identifying test smells within a project by analyzing its test coverage maps, demonstrating its superiority over existing solutions. Furthermore, we introduce eight test smells specific to Java and Python, which have not been previously detected by other methods, and showcase T5S's efficacy using eight widely-used software frameworks written in Java and Python.

This paper investigates the existence and uniqueness of solutions to a modified version of the Carathéodory-Volterra equation. This equation involves a Carathéodory mapping integrated with a function whose arguments change over time and depends on two variables. We explore the existence and uniqueness of solutions, taking into account an additional boundary condition that is imposed. The proposed modifications align the modified equation with applications in control theory, particularly in the context of linear time-invariant systems subject to carathéodory-type disturbances.

We update the \texttt{KKMCee} event generator, which creates simulations of high-energy electron-positron collisions that produce vector bosons, especially the $\Upsilon$ system, to include new data on cross-sections and branching ratios from LHC-type collisions. Additionally, we revise the \texttt{KKMCee} generator to account for the final state radiation of collinear emissions from the initial leptons and final-state vector bosons, using the soft-collinear VEGAS algorithm. This improved \texttt{KKMCee} 5.00.2 event generator maintains the full multiplicative precision of 128 bits to ensure accurate event simulations with high energy inputs.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals can provide early warnings for cardiovascular diseases. However, identifying IBIs from noisy signals is difficult, especially when they are heavily distorted by motion noise, which is common in individuals who are highly active. Researchers working on remote health monitoring and wearable devices have identified signal denoising and IBI extraction as a significant area of focus. Although various methods have been developed for ECG signal denoising, they typically do not effectively extract IBIs, which are essential for calculating heart rate variability. This paper presents an innovative approach to simultaneously denoise and extract IBIs from ECG signals by applying two weighted Orthonormal Wavelet Filter approaches. This method outperforms existing approaches in both signal denoising and IBI extraction by preserving the original signal and accurately extracting IBIs. Experimental results demonstrate the method's superiority over existing techniques in both aspects. By using this approach, medical professionals can obtain accurate denoised ECG signals and extracted inter-beat intervals for cardiovascular health monitoring.

To efficiently utilize contemporary computing systems, a crucial capability is exploring non-traditional hardware resources in an programmable manner.  A key data structure, the tensor, needs specialized approaches to extract hidden patterns when dealing with massive datasets across disciplines.  A crucial technique for working with 3-D data on computing systems is the tensor singular value decomposition (t-SVD).  Although some approaches have been suggested for computing the t-SVD, they fail to account for computing platform optimizations.  In order to develop deep learning algorithms that can operate on modern computing systems, a critical capability is a means to dynamically define matrix-based operators, such as the rank-1 tensor regression operator, in an environment that is linear and efficient.  A proposed solution introduces several novel concepts to contemporary computing systems, including a new hardware-efficient algorithm for computing t-SVD, an innovative approach to expressing the regression operator as a matrix, and a novel concept for ranking tensors according to their significance.
